extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in young-adult (YA) literature — fans, students, teachers, and aspiring YA writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating or understanding young-adult (YA) fiction, drawing on John Green's approach: what themes, characters, tone, and audience considerations make YA resonate. Useful for authors, teachers, and critics evaluating YA work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write about difficult topics in ways accessible to young readers
rubrics_metrics.description: John Green "loved the way these YA authors were able to write about difficult topics in ways that were accessible for young readers." His early exposure reviewing YA convinced him this approach was viable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on handling weighty themes (grief, illness, identity, death) with language, pacing, and explanations appropriate for adolescent readers — neither condescending nor opaque. Example: Green's novels about love and death appeal because they make those topics approachable for teens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the books you loved when you were a teenager (authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: John says: "I want to write the kind of books that I loved when I was in high school."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground your story in the kinds of feelings, questions, and narrative energy that would have spoken to you as an adolescent — authenticity of voice and empathy for the teen perspective matter more than forcing 'teen-speak.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Center teenage characters undergoing formative 'firsts'
rubrics_metrics.description: John notes teenagers are "doing so many things for the first time — like, they’re often falling in love for the first time, but they’re also asking the big questions of human existence for the first time as entities separate from their parents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus plots and character arcs on formative first experiences (first love, first serious loss, first grappling with identity or mortality). Use those firsts as catalysts for growth and thematic exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage big existential questions with earnest emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Per Green: teens are "thinking about whether there is inherent meaning to human life... the role suffering plays in human life... free will and selfhood," and they do it "with unironized emotion and enthusiasm."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't shy away from philosophical or existential themes; present them sincerely rather than ironically. Allow emotional intensity and earnest questioning to drive character motivation and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow cross-genre elements and shelf-mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Green said: "I like the way that young-adult books are published. I like that science fiction and mystery and romance all live on the shelf together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YA publishing and readership are permissive of genre-blending — you can combine romance, mystery, speculative elements, etc. Leverage cross-genre appeal rather than forcing strict genre conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider educator and librarian support as a factor in longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Green observes YA novels "tend to hang around because of support from librarians and teachers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for lasting impact, be mindful of themes, accessibility, and ethical/pedagogical considerations that encourage adoption by librarians and educators (e.g., relatable protagonists, discussion-worthy themes, classroom-appropriate handling of topics).
